text.p: Boeing executives estimated Wednesday that the aircraft manufacturer and its suppliers would spend $120 million to $140 million on changes designed to improve the safety of the worldwide 737 fleet.

In a conference call with reporters, the Boeing executives expected the changes, which are expected to be mandated by the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration for U.S.-based jets, will be completed on all 2,700 jets now flying by the end of the year 2000.
Boeing vice president Chet Ekstrand said in a statement the proposed changes were "reasonable, appropriate and technically sound."
"They will serve to make a safe airplane even safer," he said.

Mike Denton, chief project engineer on the 737, said the costs borne by Boeing and the unidentified suppliers would represent the vast majority of the expense of retrofitting the existing fleet with a new rudder limiter, servo valve and other new parts. Airline customers will pay only for labor, he said.
Denton said the new rudder limiter, the most significant of the changes being proposed by the FAA, is expected to be available beginning in October 1998 after testing and certification.
Other new parts to be required under the series of changes will be available as soon as June 1997.

The planned changes come in the wake of two unexplained crashes of 737s, including the 1994 crash of a USAir jet outside Pittsburgh that killed 132 people, but federal officials said their investigations have turned up no design flaws that could have caused the accidents.

But Denton said the rudder-limiting device, similar to one that is being incorporated by design into the next-generation family of 737s, could give pilots more chance to react in the event of a flight disruption.

"Having a limiter is going to mean that there's less rudder displacement and probably a little bit more time to take the appropriate action, but you still have to take the appropriate action," he said.
Boeing also is proposing two additional changes, including an additional parameter in the "black box" flight data recorder that will measure force applied to the rudder pedal.
Boeing also plans to go forward with new training procedures to help pilots of Boeing and other jets learn how to recover from unusual events caused by bad weather or malfunctions during flight.
Denton said the proposed changes were the result of "very comprehensive study."
"At this time we believe it's a complete set of changes, but that doesn't mean we stop," Denton said. "Zero accidents is the goal of the Boeing Company for all of our airplanes."
